span.label: Church’s thesis → a mathematical theorem
span.note: THREE PAPERS, THREE DIFFERENT VERDICTS ON WHETHER A FORMALISM CAN BE SHOWN TO CAPTURE THE INFORMAL NOTION IT REPLACES - and no type in the vocabulary can express a disagreement about what KIND OF CLAIM something is. This paper says the identification CANNOT BE MADE A THEOREM WITHOUT WEAKENING IT: a precise mathematical description of a computing device would leave open the possibility of a practical device that did not satisfy it, so the theorem would be weaker than the thesis it replaced. turing1936-computable-numbers argues it instead, enumerating three kinds of argument; tkacik2016-information-living reports a theorem that did make a vague notion precise. **`same-as` and `distinct-from` are both false here**: the three are not making one claim or two, they are ruling differently on whether the identification is the sort of thing a proof can settle. All eight edge types assert that a relation holds between two concepts. Recorded per record, each row quoting only its own paper; the cross-paper half is this paraphrase, checkable by opening the other two. Q-709, and the third case for Q-632 - which by the rule that one is an observation and three make a proposal is the point at which the gap should be put to Shir.

span.label: contradicts → the quantitative (strong) Church's thesis, that any physical computing device can be simulated by a Turing machine with at most polynomial overhead
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS WHETHER QUANTUM MECHANICS IS TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT. 'A DIGITAL COMPUTER IS GENERALLY BELIEVED TO BE AN EFFICIENT UNIVERSAL COMPUTING DEVICE; that is, it is believed able to simulate any physical computing device WITH AN INCREASE IN COMPUTATION TIME BY AT MOST A POLYNOMIAL FACTOR. THIS MAY NOT BE TRUE WHEN QUANTUM MECHANICS IS TAKEN INTO CONS[IDERATION].' The thesis is not shown false - it is shown to have a physical precondition nobody had needed to state, and the polynomial factor is what fails. A `contradicts` alone records a dispute with a computing thesis and drops the fact that the dispute is ABOUT WHICH PHYSICS THE MACHINE OBEYS. Q-502.

quantum computer
span.note: differs in: WHETHER PRECISION IS MODELLED AS A CONSTANT OR AS A RESOURCE THAT GROWS WITH THE INPUT. 'IF THIS IMPRECISION IS CONSTANT (i.e., it does not depend on the size of the input), then it is NOT KNOWN HOW TO COMPUTE ANY FUNCTIONS in polynomial time on a quantum computer that cannot also be computed in polynomial time on a classical computer ... HOWEVER, IF WE LET THE PRECISION GROW POLYNOMIALLY in the input size ... WE APPEAR TO OBTAIN A MORE POWERFUL TYPE OF COMPUTER.' The whole quantum advantage turns on that choice, not on a physical fact · strength of the relation: 0.9 — AND THE CHOICE IS DEFENDED ON USEFULNESS RATHER THAN ON TRUTH, in the paper's own words: treating precision as a large constant 'would be comparable to treating a classical digital computer as a finite automaton - since any given computer has a fixed amount of memory, THIS VIEW IS TECHNICALLY CORRECT; HOWEVER, IT IS NOT PARTICULARLY USEFUL.' Shor also says what fixes the precision available: 'not by fundamental physical laws but by the properties of the materials and the architecture with which a quantum computer is built.'
